Relational Database Mental Model
Durable state, tables, rows, schemas and invariants

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

Book 1 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                      Relational Database Mental Model

A database is durable application state
Our in-memory Todo array is useful for teaching HTTP, but it is not durable application state. A relational database gives the
application a separate system whose job is to store facts, enforce rules around those facts, answer queries and coordinate
concurrent changes.

Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations.

projects                                       tasks                                   comments

id PK                                       id PK                                      id PK
name                                    project_id FK                               task_id FK

one project                                  many tasks                              many comments

Relational database

tables + constraints + relationships + transactions

Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships.

Database, schema, table, row and column
tasks table

id                             title                            completed              project_id

1                 Learn SQL                                   false                   10

2                 Design API                                  true                    10

3                 Add persistence                             false                   11

column = attribute/type/rule      row = one stored record

Figure - Tables organize typed columns; each row stores one record that must satisfy table constraints.

Term                         Practical meaning

Database                     A PostgreSQL database that contains application schemas and objects.

Schema                       A namespace that groups database objects. PostgreSQL commonly starts with the public schema.

Table                        A relation used to store records with a defined set of columns and constraints.

Column                       A named attribute with a data type and possibly rules/defaults.

Row                          One stored record satisfying the table definition.

Constraint                   A database-enforced rule that prevents invalid states.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                 Relational Database Mental Model

The database should protect invariants
An invariant is a condition that must remain true for valid persistent data. For example, a task title may be required; an email
may need to be unique; a task may reference only an existing project. Application code can validate these conditions, but
durable database constraints provide a final line of defense when multiple clients, scripts, background jobs or future services
write to the same database.

Incoming row
candidate data

Type checks
is the value compatible?

NOT NULL / CHECK
does the value satisfy local rules?

UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY
does identity remain valid?

FOREIGN KEY
does the referenced row exist?

Accepted row
database invariant preserved

Figure - Database constraints reject invalid states before they become persistent application data.

Rows are not objects
A TypeScript object and a database row can describe the same business concept, but they are not the same thing. Objects live in
process memory and can contain methods, derived values or temporary state. Database rows are persisted values governed by
database types and constraints. Prisma later maps between these worlds; understanding the difference makes ORM behavior
less surprising.

Set-oriented thinking
SQL is designed to describe sets of rows. Instead of looping through every task in JavaScript to find incomplete items, a query
asks the database for the set matching a condition. This becomes increasingly important as data grows beyond what can be
loaded into application memory safely.
Think in sets

SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE completed = false
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

REAL-WORLD NOTE

In an HRIS, Payroll, Inventory or Procurement system, the same mental model applies: tables persist facts, constraints protect
valid relationships, and application services orchestrate workflows around that durable state.

VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING

Data Types, NULL and Constraints
How PostgreSQL represents values and rejects invalid persistent states

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

understand the database before Prisma

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 2 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                          Data Types, NULL and Constraints

Data types are part of the contract
Choosing a column type tells PostgreSQL what values can be represented and what operations make sense. Good types reduce
ambiguity and make invalid states harder to store.

Application value               Useful PostgreSQL type             Why

Task title / description        text                               Variable-length text without an arbitrary storage limit.

Completed flag                  boolean                            Represents true/false directly.

Priority number                 smallint / integer                 Numeric ordering; pair with CHECK for allowed range.

Money                           numeric(p,s)                       Exact decimal arithmetic when a monetary amount is
truly needed.

Created timestamp               timestamptz                        Timestamp with time-zone semantics normalized by
PostgreSQL.

Identifier                      bigint identity or uuid            Choice depends on system boundaries and identity
strategy.

Structured flexible metadata    jsonb                              Useful when structure is genuinely variable; not a
substitute for normal columns.

Prefer modern identity columns for generated numeric IDs
Generated identity example

CREATE TABLE practice_tasks (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
title text NOT NULL
);

PostgreSQL supports identity columns as the SQL-standard way to generate values. The course uses them for fundamentals.
Later, TaskFlow may use UUIDs where that better matches authentication or distributed identity requirements.

NULL means missing/unknown, not empty
NULL is not the same as an empty string, zero or false. Comparisons involving NULL require special reasoning. Use IS NULL
and IS NOT NULL, not = NULL.
Correct NULL check

SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE due_at IS NULL;

Three-valued logic

SQL conditions can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. A comparison such as due_at = NULL does not mean what
JavaScript developers often expect.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                    Data Types, NULL and Constraints

Constraints encode durable rules
Incoming row
candidate data

Type checks
is the value compatible?

NOT NULL / CHECK
does the value satisfy local rules?

UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY
does identity remain valid?

FOREIGN KEY
does the referenced row exist?

Accepted row
database invariant preserved

Figure - Database constraints reject invalid states before they become persistent application data.

Constraint                         Protects

NOT NULL                           A required value cannot be absent.

CHECK                              A value or combination of values must satisfy an expression.

UNIQUE                             No two rows may share the constrained value combination.

PRIMARY KEY                        The table has one chosen unique non-null row identity.

FOREIGN KEY                        A relationship must point to a valid referenced row (unless nullable by design).

A small constraint-rich table

CREATE TABLE practice_tasks (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
title text NOT NULL,
completed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 2,
due_at timestamptz,
CONSTRAINT practice_tasks_priority_check
CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 3)
);

Defaults are convenience, constraints are rules
A default supplies a value when an INSERT omits that column. It does not make arbitrary incoming values valid. A CHECK or
other constraint is what rejects invalid persisted values. Keep those responsibilities separate.

Do not use JSON for everything
PostgreSQL has excellent jsonb support, but a flexible JSON document is not automatically the best model for strongly related
business data. If the application routinely filters, joins or constrains a field, a normal typed column is usually easier to validate,
query and index. JSON is useful when the domain is genuinely document-like or extensible.

VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING

Keys, Relationships and Joins
Identity, referential integrity and relational reads

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

understand the database before Prisma

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 3 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                             Keys, Relationships and Joins

Primary keys answer: which row?
A primary key identifies each row uniquely and cannot be NULL. PostgreSQL automatically creates a unique B-tree index for
the primary-key columns. The key is both a data-integrity rule and an efficient lookup path.
Primary key

CREATE TABLE projects (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
name text NOT NULL
);

Foreign keys answer: does this relationship exist?
A foreign key requires values in the referencing column to match a key in another table. This prevents a task from claiming to
belong to a project that does not exist.
Foreign key

CREATE TABLE tasks (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
project_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
title text NOT NULL
);

Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations.

projects                                      tasks                                     comments

id PK                                       id PK                                         id PK
name                                    project_id FK                                  task_id FK

one project                                 many tasks                                many comments

Relational database

tables + constraints + relationships + transactions

Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships.

Foreign-key actions are domain decisions
Action                              Meaning                                    Typical question

NO ACTION / RESTRICT                Prevent parent change/delete when          Should a project be deletable while tasks still exist?
dependent rows would be invalid.

CASCADE                             Propagate parent delete/update to          Are child rows meaningless without the parent?
related rows.

SET NULL                            Remove the relationship while              Can a task exist without a project?
preserving the child row.

Do not cargo-cult CASCADE

Cascade behavior can be correct, but it can also turn one delete into a large irreversible data change. Choose referential actions
from business meaning, not convenience.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                Keys, Relationships and Joins

One-to-many and many-to-many
A project has many tasks when tasks.project_id references projects.id. A many-to-many relationship usually becomes an
explicit join table containing two foreign keys, often with a composite primary key or unique constraint.
Many-to-many join table

CREATE TABLE task_labels (
task_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks(id),
label_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES labels(id),
PRIMARY KEY (task_id, label_id)
);

JOIN reads related facts
Inner join

SELECT
t.id,
t.title,
p.name AS project_name
FROM tasks AS t
JOIN projects AS p ON p.id = t.project_id
ORDER BY t.id;

The join condition states how rows relate. An INNER JOIN returns rows that have matches on both sides. A LEFT JOIN keeps
rows from the left side even when no right-side match exists. Choosing a join is therefore part of the question being asked, not
merely SQL syntax.

Question                                                     Useful join

Show tasks only when their project exists                    INNER JOIN

Show every project, including projects with zero tasks       LEFT JOIN from projects to tasks

Show every task and optional assignee details                LEFT JOIN when assignee is nullable

Foreign keys and indexes are different responsibilities
The referenced primary/unique key is indexed, but PostgreSQL does not automatically create an index on the referencing
foreign-key column. If the application frequently joins, filters, updates or deletes through that foreign key, an index on the
referencing column is often useful. We justify it from query patterns rather than from habit.

SQL CRUD, Filtering and Aggregates
Read and change rows with deliberate query semantics

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

understand the database before Prisma

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 4 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                SQL CRUD, Filtering and Aggregates

CRUD in SQL is explicit data manipulation
Our HTTP API uses GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE. The database has a different language. SQL commands describe data
retrieval and changes. Prisma later translates typed method calls into SQL concepts like these.

INSERT - create persistent rows
INSERT with RETURNING

INSERT INTO projects (name)
VALUES ('Full Stack Course')
RETURNING id, name;

RETURNING lets PostgreSQL return the inserted or modified rows without a second SELECT. This is useful for generated
IDs and server-side defaults.

SELECT - ask a question
Filtered and ordered query

SELECT id, title, completed
FROM tasks
WHERE project_id = 10
AND completed = false
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

FROM / JOIN
which rows and relationships participate?

WHERE
which rows survive filtering?

GROUP BY
which rows become groups?

HAVING
which groups survive?

SELECT
which expressions are returned?

ORDER BY / LIMIT
how is the final result shaped?

Figure - A useful conceptual order for reasoning about SELECT queries. SQL syntax is written in a different order, but this mental pipeline
helps debugging.

UPDATE - change selected rows
Targeted update

UPDATE tasks
SET completed = true,
completed_at = now()
WHERE id = 42
RETURNING id, completed, completed_at;

DELETE - remove selected rows
Targeted delete

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                   SQL CRUD, Filtering and Aggregates

DELETE FROM tasks
WHERE id = 42
RETURNING id;

DANGEROUS DIFFERENCE

UPDATE tasks SET completed = true; affects every row. DELETE FROM tasks; deletes every row. The absence of WHERE
is valid SQL, which is why query review and transactions matter.

Filtering operators you will use constantly
Pattern                             Example

Equality                            status = 'OPEN'

Range                               priority >= 2

Set membership                      status IN ('OPEN', 'BLOCKED')

Pattern matching                    title ILIKE '%postgres%'

Null test                           due_at IS NULL

Date/time comparison                created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'

Aggregates answer questions across rows
Aggregate query

SELECT
project_id,
count(*) AS open_task_count
FROM tasks
WHERE completed = false
GROUP BY project_id
HAVING count(*) >= 5
ORDER BY open_task_count DESC;

WHERE filters rows before grouping. GROUP BY creates groups. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. This distinction
becomes important for dashboards and reports.

Select only what the caller needs
During learning it is tempting to write SELECT * everywhere. Production queries are often clearer and more stable when they
select the columns the caller actually needs. Explicit projections also make API contracts and performance tradeoffs more
visible.

Transactions, Indexes and Concurrency
Atomic workflows, query access paths and multi-user thinking

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 5 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                              Transactions, Indexes and Concurrency

Transactions protect multi-step invariants
Many application workflows require several database changes to succeed together. If one succeeds and another fails, the
database can end up representing a business state that should never exist. A transaction groups the changes into one unit of
work.

A transaction groups related changes into one unit of work.
BEGIN

start transaction

UPDATE task                                        INSERT activity

mark complete                                        record event

COMMIT                                                   ROLLBACK

all changes become durable                                discard transaction changes

Figure - COMMIT makes the unit succeed; ROLLBACK abandons it when the workflow cannot be completed safely.

Successful transaction

BEGIN;

UPDATE tasks
SET completed = true
WHERE id = 42;

INSERT INTO activity_log (task_id, action)
VALUES (42, 'completed');

COMMIT;

Abandon changes

BEGIN;
-- perform several related changes
-- something fails or business rule is not satisfied
ROLLBACK;

ACID as an application developer
Property                  Practical meaning

Atomicity                 The transaction commits as one unit or rolls back as one unit.

Consistency               Constraints and application rules move the database between valid states.

Isolation                 Concurrent transactions are controlled so their interaction has defined behavior.

Durability                Committed changes survive normal process/server failures according to PostgreSQL durability
mechanisms.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                              Transactions, Indexes and Concurrency

Concurrency means other users exist
A single-user tutorial can pretend no one else changes data between your read and write. Production systems cannot.
PostgreSQL uses MVCC and transaction isolation to coordinate concurrent access. You do not need deep database-internals
knowledge yet, but you must stop assuming that a value you read will remain unchanged until your later UPDATE.

Later application pattern

Optimistic concurrency checks, row locks and carefully scoped transactions exist because multiple requests can race. We
introduce advanced patterns only when TaskFlow has workflows that actually need them.

Indexes are access paths
Indexes are access paths - not free speed buttons.

Without useful index                                                          With useful B-tree

scan many table rows                                                   navigate matching key range

Trade-off

faster reads can mean more storage and write work

Figure - An index can reduce lookup work when it matches the query pattern, but it has storage and maintenance cost.

By default, CREATE INDEX creates a B-tree index, which is appropriate for many equality and range searches. An index helps
only when it matches how the application searches or orders data. It also consumes storage and must be maintained when rows
are inserted, updated or deleted.
Example indexes

CREATE INDEX tasks_project_id_idx
ON tasks (project_id);

CREATE INDEX tasks_project_open_idx
ON tasks (project_id, completed);

Why foreign-key columns often need deliberate indexes
A foreign-key declaration does not automatically index the referencing column in PostgreSQL. If TaskFlow frequently finds
tasks by project_id or PostgreSQL must locate child rows while checking a parent change/delete, an index can reduce the work.
The correct index still depends on the actual workload.

Composite index order matters
An index on (project_id, completed) is not equivalent to one on (completed, project_id). Index column order should reflect
the query patterns, selectivity and ordering requirements. Do not collect indexes as decorations.

Normalization and Schema Evolution
Design durable facts and change schemas without losing the mental model

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

understand the database before Prisma

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 6 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                        Normalization and Schema Evolution

Normalization is about one durable fact in one sensible place

Bad repeated data                                                           Separated facts

task row repeats project name                                                  projects, users, tasks
and owner email                                                             linked by keys

Goal

store each durable fact in a sensible place;
join related facts when reading

Figure - Normalization reduces contradictory copies of the same fact; it is a design tool, not a rule to maximize table count.

Suppose every task row stores project_name and project_owner_email. Renaming the project would require updating many task
rows; missing one creates contradictory copies of the same fact. A normalized model stores the project facts once and lets tasks
reference the project.

The useful idea behind 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
Form                     Practical intuition

1NF                      Store values in a queryable table shape; avoid repeating groups packed into one column.

2NF                      When a key has multiple columns, non-key facts should depend on the whole key.

3NF                      Non-key facts should describe the row identified by the key, not another non-key fact.

You do not need to chant normal forms while coding. The professional habit is to ask: What fact does this row represent?
Where is that fact authoritative? What contradictions become possible if I duplicate it?

Denormalization is a trade-off, not a failure
Sometimes duplicated or precomputed data is deliberately introduced for performance, reporting or historical snapshots. That is
a design decision with synchronization costs. First understand the normalized source of truth; then denormalize when a
measured requirement justifies it.

Schema evolution is inevitable
Production schemas change as requirements change. PostgreSQL supports ALTER TABLE operations, but application teams
normally record schema changes as versioned migrations so environments can advance in a repeatable order. Phase 09 shows
how Prisma migrations become that change history for TaskFlow.
Schema evolution examples

ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN due_at timestamptz;

ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD CONSTRAINT tasks_title_not_blank
CHECK (length(btrim(title)) > 0);

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                            Normalization and Schema Evolution

A migration is not just the final schema
The final schema answers what the database looks like now. Migration history answers how an existing database gets from an
older valid state to the new valid state. Those are different concerns.

Renames, destructive changes and data backfills
●    Adding a nullable column is usually easier than immediately adding a required column to a table that already contains rows.
●    Changing a column type can require conversion and may lock or rewrite data depending on the operation.
●    Dropping a column destroys stored information; production migrations need backups, rollout planning and application
compatibility.
●    Large data backfills are operational work, not merely schema syntax.
●    Application deployment and database migration order can matter when old and new application versions overlap.

Preview of Prisma migrations

Prisma will later generate migration SQL for many schema changes, but generated SQL is still database change code. A
professional developer reviews what it will do instead of treating migrations as a magic button.

Book 7 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                          TaskFlow Data Modeling Lab

TaskFlow practice schema - not the final production schema
This lab uses a deliberately small relational model so you can reason about real application questions. Phase 10 will design the
final TaskFlow model after Supabase and Prisma are available. Do not prematurely copy this practice schema into production.

Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations.

projects                                    tasks                                    comments

id PK                                      id PK                                      id PK
name                                   project_id FK                               task_id FK

one project                               many tasks                             many comments

Relational database

tables + constraints + relationships + transactions

Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships.

Practice schema

CREATE TABLE practice_projects (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
name text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE practice_tasks (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
project_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES practice_projects(id),
title text NOT NULL,
completed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 2 CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 3),
due_at timestamptz,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Turn product questions into relational questions
Product question                                   Database question

Show open tasks for one project                    Filter practice_tasks by project_id and completed.

Show project name beside each task                 Join tasks to projects through project_id.

Count open tasks per project                       Filter, group by project and count.

Delete a project                                   What should happen to its tasks? Choose FK action from product meaning.

Sort upcoming work                                 Order by due_at while deciding how NULL due dates should appear.

Find high-priority incomplete tasks quickly        Which query pattern might justify a composite index?

Seed practice rows
Practice seed data

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                                       TaskFlow Data Modeling Lab

INSERT INTO practice_projects (name)
VALUES ('Course'), ('Portfolio')
RETURNING id, name;

INSERT INTO practice_tasks (project_id, title, priority)
VALUES
(1, 'Learn relational modeling', 1),
(1, 'Practice joins', 2),
(2, 'Build portfolio project', 1);

Query 1 - open tasks for a project
Project task list

SELECT id, title, priority
FROM practice_tasks
WHERE project_id = 1
AND completed = false
ORDER BY priority, created_at;

Query 2 - project dashboard counts
Simple project dashboard

SELECT
p.id,
p.name,
count(t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.completed = false) AS open_tasks,
count(t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.completed = true) AS done_tasks
FROM practice_projects AS p
LEFT JOIN practice_tasks AS t ON t.project_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;

Add an index because of a query, not because of a column
Index tied to a repeated query pattern

CREATE INDEX practice_tasks_project_completed_idx
ON practice_tasks (project_id, completed);

This index is justifiable if TaskFlow repeatedly requests tasks by project and completion state. It is not automatically justified
merely because those columns exist.

Think before final schema design
●    Should project names be globally unique, or only unique inside a workspace? The answer changes the UNIQUE constraint.
●    Should deleting a project delete tasks, prevent deletion, archive the project, or move tasks elsewhere? This changes
referential and application behavior.
●    Should priority be numeric, an enum-like text value, or its own table? Choose based on domain requirements, not aesthetic
preference.
●    Should tasks have one assignee or many? That changes relationship cardinality.
●    Should completed_at be derived from completed, or stored as historical information? The business meaning matters.

ENGINEERING HABIT

Schema design is product design expressed as persistent rules. Every key, nullability choice, constraint and cascade policy
encodes assumptions about the domain.

SQL Safety, Debugging and Practical
Workflow
Operate the database carefully and isolate failures by layer

Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic.

Application                            SQL / ORM                              PostgreSQL

NestJS business logic                   database commands                     durable relational state

Phase 07 focus

understand the database before Prisma

Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning.

Book 8 of Phase 07

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                       SQL Safety, Debugging and Practical Workflow

SQL is powerful enough to damage data
The same language that updates one Todo can update every Todo. Professional database work therefore combines precise SQL
with observability, transactions, backups, permissions and review discipline.

Preview before update or delete
Observe the target set first

SELECT id, title, completed
FROM tasks
WHERE project_id = 10
AND completed = false;

-- After verifying the target set:
UPDATE tasks
SET completed = true
WHERE project_id = 10
AND completed = false
RETURNING id, title;

Production safety

For high-impact operations, use an explicit transaction, inspect the affected rows, and commit only when the result matches your
intention. On production systems, permissions and operational procedures should further limit dangerous direct writes.

Parameterized queries prevent data from becoming SQL
code
Application code should not build SQL by concatenating untrusted strings. Database drivers and ORMs support parameterized
queries so user input is transmitted as data rather than executable SQL structure. Prisma later handles normal parameterization
for us, but understanding the security boundary still matters.
Parameter placeholder concept

-- Conceptual parameterized SQL
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE title ILIKE $1;

-- $1 is a bound parameter, not concatenated SQL text.

Debug SQL layer by layer
1      Schema: Does the table/column actually exist, and is the expected migration applied?
2      Type: Are values compatible with the target column type?
3      Constraint: Which NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY rule rejected the write?
4      Data: Does the row you expect actually exist?
5      Query: Does WHERE match the rows you think it matches?
6      Transaction: Is the transaction committed, rolled back, blocked or already failed?
7      Plan/performance: Is the query logically correct but doing far more work than expected?

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07                                                         SQL Safety, Debugging and Practical Workflow

Common PostgreSQL errors are useful evidence
Failure                                             What to investigate

duplicate key violates unique constraint            Which uniqueness rule exists? Is the duplicate expected or a race?

violates foreign key constraint                     Does the referenced parent exist? Is the relationship ID correct?

null value violates not-null constraint             Which required field was omitted? Should it truly be required?

violates check constraint                           Which domain rule rejected the candidate value?

relation does not exist                             Wrong schema/database, missing migration or misspelled object?

column does not exist                               Schema mismatch, typo or application ahead of database migration?

Use psql as an observable client when available
Illustrative psql workflow

psql "$env:DATABASE_URL"

\dt
\d practice_tasks
SELECT current_database();

Phase 08 will provide the real Supabase connection context. The important idea now is that psql is simply another PostgreSQL
client: it lets you inspect schema and execute SQL without involving NestJS or Prisma, which is invaluable for isolating
database-layer problems.

Do not optimize the wrong query
●     First prove the query returns the correct rows.
●     Then measure the workload and inspect EXPLAIN output.
●     Add or adjust an index because of repeated query patterns, not because a blog post says every foreign key must have the
same index shape.
●     Remember that indexes speed some reads while increasing storage and write maintenance.
●     Do not use application-side loops to replace joins/aggregates when the database can answer the set-based question directly.

Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan, not to guess
Inspect a query plan

EXPLAIN
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE project_id = 10
AND completed = false;

Performance rule

Measure before optimizing. A sequential scan on a tiny table can be completely reasonable. The goal is not to force index usage;
the goal is to give PostgreSQL good data structures and let the planner choose an efficient plan.

Database debugging boundary

If a SELECT returns the wrong rows in psql, the problem is below Next.js and NestJS. If the SQL is correct in psql but the API
returns something else, move one layer upward. This boundary-based method prevents random full-stack debugging.

Active recall - explain before looking back
●      What is the difference between a database, schema, table, row and column?
●      Why is NULL not equivalent to an empty string or false?
●      What invariant does a primary key protect?
●      What invariant does a foreign key protect?

Level 1 - Follow

project foreign key.
2      Write INSERT statements for two projects and three tasks.
3      Write a SELECT for incomplete tasks in one project ordered by priority.
4      Write an UPDATE that completes exactly one task and returns the modified row.
5      Write a DELETE that removes exactly one task and returns its id.

Level 2 - Modify
1      Add an optional due_at timestamptz column and query only tasks with a due date.
2      Add a CHECK constraint that allows priority values 1 through 3.
3      Add a UNIQUE rule appropriate for a practice label table.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 07: PostgreSQL Fundamentals

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Business invariant -> table design -> key/constraint -> SQL query -> query plan/index -> transaction -> durable rows

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Treating IDs as the only integrity mechanism
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Adding indexes without understanding query patterns
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.
